title: What Scripture says of his appearance
source_text: Ἑξῆς τούτοις λέγει ὅτι ἐπειδὴ θεῖον πνεῦμα ἦν ἐν σώματι, πάντως τι παραλλάττειν αὐτὸ τῶν λοιπῶν ἐχρῆν (ἢ) κατὰ μέγεθος ἢ κάλλος ἢ ἀλκὴν ἢ φωνὴν ἢ κατάπληξιν ἢ πειθώ. ἀμήχανον γὰρ ὅτῳ θεῖόν τι πλέον τῶν ἄλλων προσῆν μηδὲν ἄλλου διαφέρειν· τοῦτο δὲ οὐδὲν ἄλλου διέφερεν, ἀλλ᾿, ὥς φασι, μικρὸν καὶ δυσειδὲς καὶ ἀγεννὲς ἦν. φαίνεται δὴ καὶ ἐν τούτοις ὅτι, ἐὰν μὲν κατηγορεῖν θέλῃ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, ὡς πιστεύων ταῖς παρέχειν δοκούσαις αὐτῷ γραφαῖς ἀφορμὰς κατηγορίας λέγει τὰ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν· ὅπου δὲ κατὰ τὰς αὐτὰς γραφὰς δόξαι ἄν τις τὰ ἐναντία λέγεσθαι τοῖς εἰς κατηγορίαν παραλαμβανομένοις, ταῦτα οὐδὲ προσποιεῖται εἰδέναι. ὁμολογουμένως τοίνυν γέγραπται τὰ περὶ τοῦ δυσειδὲς γεγονέναι τὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ σῶμα, οὐ μὴν ὡς ἐκτέθειται καὶ ἀγεννὲς. οὐδὲ σαφῶς δηλοῦται ὅτι μικρὸν ἦν. ἔχει δὲ ἡ λέξις οὕτως παρὰ τῷ Ἡσαΐᾳ ἀναγεγραμμένη, προφητεύοντι αὐτὸν ἐπιδημήσοντα τοῖς πολλοῖς οὐκ ἐν ὡραίῳ εἴδει οὐδέ τινι ὑπερέχοντι κάλλει· „κύριε, τίς ἐπίστευσε τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν; καὶ ὁ βραχίων κυρίου τίνι ἀπεκαλύφθη; ἀνηγγείλαμεν ἐναντίον αὐτοῦ ὡς παιδίον, ὡς ῥίζα ἐν γῇ διψώσῃ· οὐκ ἔστιν εἶδος αὐτῷ (οὐδὲ δόξα· καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος) οὐδὲ κάλλος· ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον, ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων. “ ἆρ᾿ οὖν τούτων μὲν ὁ Κέλσος ἤκουεν, ἐπεὶ ᾤετο αὐτῷ χρήσιμα εἶναι εἰς τὸ κατηγορεῖσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν, οὐκέτι δὲ προσέσχε τοῖς λεγομένοις ἐν τεσσαρακοστῷ τετάρτῳ ψαλμῷ, τίνα τρόπον λέγεται· „περίζωσαι τὴν ῥομφαίαν σου ἐπὶ τὸν μηρόν σου, δυνατὲ, τῇ ὡραιότητί σου καὶ τῷ κάλλει σου· καὶ ἔντεινον καὶ κατευοδοῦ καὶ βασίλευε;“
pass_a_gloss: Next to these he says that (ὅτι): 'Since a divine spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) was in a body, it must (ἐχρῆν) altogether (πάντως) differ (παραλλάττειν) somewhat from the rest, either in size (μέγεθος) or beauty (κάλλος) or strength (ἀλκή) or voice (φωνή) or striking awe (κατάπληξις) or persuasion (πειθώ). For it is impossible (ἀμήχανον) that one to whom something divine belonged more than to others should differ in nothing from another; but this [body] differed in nothing from another, but, as they say, was small (μικρόν) and ill-formed (δυσειδές) and low-born/ignoble (ἀγεννές).' It appears (φαίνεται) also in these that, if he wishes to accuse (κατηγορεῖν) Jesus, as believing the writings (γραφαῖς) that seem to provide him starting points (ἀφορμάς) of accusation, he states the things from them; but where according to the same writings one might think the opposite is said to the things taken up for accusation, these he does not even pretend (προσποιεῖται) to know. Admittedly (ὁμολογουμένως) then it is written about the body of Jesus having been ill-formed, not however, as he has set out, also ignoble; nor is it clearly shown that it was small. The wording (λέξις) runs thus, recorded in Isaiah, prophesying him about to come to stay among (ἐπιδημήσοντα) the many not in a comely (ὡραίῳ) form (εἴδει) nor in any surpassing (ὑπερέχοντι) beauty: 'Lord, who believed our hearing/report (ἀκοῇ)? and the arm (βραχίων) of the Lord, to whom was it revealed (ἀπεκαλύφθη)? We announced (ἀνηγγείλαμεν) before him as a little child (παιδίον), as a root (ῥίζα) in thirsty (διψώσῃ) earth; he has no form (εἶδος) [nor glory (δόξα); and we saw him, and he had no form] nor beauty; but his form dishonoured (ἄτιμον), failing (ἐκλεῖπον) beside (παρά) the sons of men.' Did Celsus then hear these, since he thought them useful to him for Jesus' being accused, but no longer attend (προσέσχε) to the things said in the forty-fourth psalm, in what manner it is said: 'Gird (περίζωσαι) your broadsword (ῥομφαίαν) on your thigh (μηρόν), mighty one (δυνατέ), in your comeliness (ὡραιότητι) and your beauty; and bend/press on (ἔντεινον) and prosper (κατευοδοῦ) and reign (βασίλευε)'?
pass_b_english: After this he says: “Since a divine spirit was in a body, it surely ought to have differed somewhat from the rest, in size or beauty or strength or voice or power to astonish or persuasiveness. For it is impossible that one to whom something divine belonged beyond others should differ in nothing from another. Yet this body differed in nothing from another, but, as they say, was small and ugly and ignoble.”

Here too it is plain that when he wants to accuse Jesus, he cites what comes from the Scriptures that seem to him to offer grounds for accusation, as if he believed them; but where, by the same Scriptures, one might think the opposite is said to what he takes up for his accusation, he does not even pretend to know it.

It is admitted, then, that it is written that the body of Jesus was ugly; not, however, that it was ignoble too, as he has set it out, nor is it clearly shown that it was small. The passage recorded in Isaiah, who prophesies that he would come among the many not in a comely form nor with any surpassing beauty, reads as follows: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground. He has no form nor glory; and we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short compared with the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:1–3).

Did Celsus, then, listen to these words because he thought them useful for accusing Jesus, but pay no attention to what is said in the forty-fourth psalm (Psalm 45 in English Bibles), and how it is said: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty; and press on, and prosper, and reign” (Psalm 45:3–4)?

choices.choice: Celsus’s words are introduced with λέγει ὅτι but then run on in direct form (ἐχρῆν, ἀμήχανον γάρ), so they are quoted as his words. θεῖον πνεῦμα in Celsus’s mouth left lower case (‘a divine spirit’). κατάπληξις rendered ‘power to astonish’. Isaiah 53:1-3 is quoted from the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew (e.g. ‘we announced before him as a child’); translated as Origen quotes it. The parenthesis οὐδὲ δόξα· καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος is an editorial supplement in Koetschau’s text, matching the LXX; translated. ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων rendered ‘falling short compared with the sons of men’ and kept the same in 6.76-77, where Origen builds on παρά. LXX Psalm 44:4-5 = English Psalm 45:3-4; the in-text ‘forty-fourth psalm’ is kept as Origen counts it with the English number added, following earlier chunks. ἔντεινον has no object in the Greek (often understood as ‘bend [the bow]’); rendered ‘press on’ to avoid adding a word.
δυσειδές made consistent: Origen's 'unsightly' -> 'ugly' to match Celsus's word
'The passage stands written in Isaiah' (archaic) -> 'The passage recorded in Isaiah ... reads as follows'
checked: Isaiah 53:1-3 LXX wording; LXX Psalm 44:4-5 = English Psalm 45:3-4
